description: Replace unstructured interviews with paid work samples. Schmidt and Hunter report that work samples predict job performance at about 0.54 correlation, against about 0.38 for unstructured interviews. Design a 4 to 8 hour simulation of the real job, pay candidates for their time, and score the output blindly against a rubric fixed before anyone submits.

steps.description: Identify the tasks that actually fill the working week for this role, ignoring the job posting. Shadow or interview a current holder, log what they do, rank tasks by impact on team output, and keep the two or three highest-impact tasks that can be simulated without internal systems.

inputs.name: role-title
inputs.desc: The title of the role being hired for

inputs.name: current-holder-log
inputs.desc: A log from shadowing or interviewing someone currently in the role, recording their actual tasks

outputs.name: ranked-task-list
outputs.desc: Every task the current holder performs, ranked by impact on team output rather than by hours spent

outputs.name: work-sample-candidate-tasks
outputs.desc: The two or three highest-impact tasks that can be simulated without proprietary data, flagged as work sample candidates

process: List every task the current holder performed over one full working week, with estimated hours for each.
Rate each task on impact: if it were done poorly, how much would the team suffer? Rank by impact, not by hours.
Keep the two or three highest-impact tasks that can be simulated without proprietary data or internal tools. If the top task needs internal systems, substitute a public equivalent.
Record which tasks you dropped and why, so the work sample cannot be accused of testing the wrong thing.

steps.description: Turn the candidate tasks into a self-contained 4 to 8 hour simulation. The brief must be completable by someone who does not know your internal systems, must include every piece of context needed to start, and must mirror the real work rather than a puzzle.

inputs.name: ranked-task-list
inputs.desc: The impact-ranked task list from the audit

outputs.name: work-sample-brief
outputs.desc: The complete task brief given to candidates, with all context, the deliverable, and the time scope

outputs.name: time-and-materials-spec
outputs.desc: The expected hours and the reference materials provided, confirmed to expose no private information

process: Write the brief as if assigning the task to a new hire on day one, including every piece of context they need. If a candidate would have to ask a clarifying question to begin, the brief is incomplete.
Set the scope to 4 to 8 hours of work. Shorter samples give too little signal; longer ones impose too much on the candidate.
List the materials you provide, such as data files and reference documents, and confirm none expose private information.
Define the exact deliverable: what the candidate submits, in what format, and by when.

steps.description: Pay candidates for the work sample at the role's hourly rate. Unpaid samples select for people who can afford to work for free, which is a bias rather than a filter. Fix the amount, the payment timing, and the ownership of the output up front.

inputs.name: work-sample-brief
inputs.desc: The task brief candidates will receive

inputs.name: time-and-materials-spec
inputs.desc: The expected hours and provided materials

outputs.name: compensation-terms
outputs.desc: The fixed payment amount, when it is paid, and the statement that output stays the candidate's property

outputs.name: candidate-instructions
outputs.desc: The candidate-facing package: the brief, the pay, the deadline, and a contact for questions

process: Set pay at the role's loaded hourly rate times the expected hours, and state the fixed amount up front.
Pay on submission, not on advancement. The payment is for the candidate's time, whether or not they are hired.
State that any work product remains the candidate's property and will not be used by the company, which keeps the sample fair and avoids free labor.
Write the candidate-facing instructions: the brief, the pay, the deadline, and who to contact with questions.

steps.description: Build the scoring rubric before any candidate submits, so it cannot be reverse-engineered from the first submission. Define four to six dimensions, each on a one to five scale with concrete anchors, weighted by importance to the role.

inputs.name: compensation-terms
inputs.desc: The payment terms for the sample

outputs.name: scoring-rubric
outputs.desc: Four to six weighted dimensions, each with concrete anchors at levels one, three, and five

outputs.name: scorer-guide
outputs.desc: Instructions for scorers: rate each dimension independently and record a one-line reason for every score

process: Choose four to six dimensions that separate strong work from mediocre work on this task, such as accuracy, thoroughness, clarity, and judgment under ambiguity.
For each dimension, write concrete anchors for levels one, three, and five. Level one is unacceptable, level three is competent, level five is exceptional.
Weight the dimensions. If accuracy matters twice as much as formatting, give it double weight.
Write the scorer guide: score each dimension on its own, do not let one strong dimension inflate the others, and record a one-line reason for each score.

steps.description: Strip candidate identity from every submission before scoring, and have each scorer rate independently before any discussion. Anonymizing removes the halo of a strong resume or a familiar name.

outputs.name: blinding-steps
outputs.desc: The step-by-step process a non-scoring coordinator uses to strip identity and assign random codes

outputs.name: inter-rater-resolution
outputs.desc: How scorers resolve disagreements of more than one point on a dimension through discussion and re-scoring

process: A coordinator who does not score removes names, contact details, and identifying metadata from each submission and assigns a random four-digit code.
Each scorer rates all anonymized submissions alone, using the rubric, with no discussion until every score is in.
Where two scorers differ by more than one point on any dimension, they discuss that dimension and re-score. The aim is calibration, not forced agreement.
Record final scores by code, and reveal identities only after scoring is complete.

steps.description: Collect interviewer predictions separately and compare them against the work sample scores. Place each candidate on a grid of high or low work sample against high or low interview impression. The divergent cases teach you the most.

outputs.name: signal-comparison-grid
outputs.desc: Each candidate placed on a grid of work sample score against interview impression

outputs.name: divergence-cases
outputs.desc: The candidates where the two signals disagree, each with a recommendation

process: After any interview, have each interviewer record a prediction (succeed, unsure, or not) with a one-line reason, before seeing the work sample scores.
Plot each candidate with the work sample score on one axis and the interview impression on the other.
A high sample with a low interview often marks a strong hire that a conventional process would reject on surface factors. Investigate what drove the low impression.
A low sample with a high interview marks someone who interviews well but may underperform. Investigate before advancing them.

steps.description: After hires are made, track the correlation between work sample scores and real performance at six and twelve months. A weak correlation means the sample is testing the wrong task. Fix the task, not the scoring.

inputs.name: signal-comparison-grid
inputs.desc: The grid of work sample against interview signals

outputs.name: validity-report
outputs.desc: The correlation between work sample scores and actual performance at six and twelve months

outputs.name: work-sample-revision-plan
outputs.desc: The specific change to the task, materials, or rubric indicated by the validity data

process: At six months, collect the manager's performance rating for each hire and compare it against their work sample score.
At twelve months, repeat. The twelve-month figure is the one that matters.
If the correlation sits below 0.40, revisit the task audit and pick a different task to simulate.
Track the divergent cases separately: did the high-sample, low-interview hires succeed? If so, the sample saved you from a wrong rejection.

description: Learn what to hire for by studying your best people, not by copying a credential list. Interview three to five top performers to find what they do differently day to day, which skills they use that the job posting never mentioned, and which behaviors set them apart. Rewrite the requirements around what the best people actually do.

steps.description: Identify the top three to five performers using output signals rather than manager ratings, which measure who the manager likes. If output data is thin, use peer nomination.

inputs.name: role-or-team
inputs.desc: The role or team you are building the hiring profile for

inputs.name: performance-signal
inputs.desc: Available output data or the basis for peer nomination

outputs.name: top-performer-set
outputs.desc: The three to five top performers chosen, with the data behind each choice

outputs.name: selection-rationale
outputs.desc: Which method was used, output signal or peer nomination, and why

process: Collect output signals for everyone in the role: results shipped, revenue produced, cases resolved, whatever the role is measured by.
Rank by the output signal. The top three to five are your interview subjects.
If output data is unreliable, ask each team member privately to name two people they would want on a critical project, and take the most-named.
Record which method you used, so you can revisit it if the resulting profile does not predict well.

steps.description: Shadow or closely interview each top performer about a normal working day. The goal is to see what they actually do hour to hour, not what their job description claims.

outputs.name: daily-activity-log
outputs.desc: For each performer, what they actually do across a representative day, grouped into activities

outputs.name: time-allocation-map
outputs.desc: Where the real working hours go for the best people, including activities the posting never mentions

process: For each top performer, log how they spend a representative day or two, grouped into activities.
Note where they spend time that the job posting does not mention at all.
Record the order in which they do things and what they deliberately choose not to do.
Build a map that shows where the real hours go for the best people.

steps.description: Interview each top performer to surface what sets them apart. Most will first say they just work hard. Push past that to specific actions and to the skills they use daily that no one told them to learn.

outputs.name: differentiating-behaviors
outputs.desc: The concrete actions and habits that separate top performers from their peers

outputs.name: hidden-skill-list
outputs.desc: Skills the performers use daily that were never named when they were hired

process: Ask each performer what they do that colleagues who perform less well do not do, pushing for concrete actions rather than traits.
When they say they work hard or ask questions, ask what specifically they ask about and who they seek out.
Ask what skill they use every day that was not mentioned when they were hired.
Ask what they would spend the most time on if they had one week to train their replacement; the answer is usually a hidden skill.
Record concrete behaviors and skills, discarding vague self-descriptions.

steps.description: Compare what the job posting asks for against what the top performers actually do. Many listed credentials predict nothing, and several real requirements never appear in the posting.

inputs.name: differentiating-behaviors
inputs.desc: The behaviors that set top performers apart

inputs.name: hidden-skill-list
inputs.desc: The skills they use that the posting omits

outputs.name: posting-reality-gap
outputs.desc: The real requirements that the current posting leaves out

outputs.name: credential-noise-list
outputs.desc: The listed requirements that no top performer's success actually depends on

process: Lay the current job posting next to the differentiating behaviors and hidden skills.
Mark each posting requirement: does any top performer's success actually depend on it? If not, it is credential noise.
Mark each behavior or hidden skill the posting never mentions; these are the missing real requirements.
Produce two lists: the gap of real requirements absent from the posting, and the noise of listed requirements that predict nothing.

steps.description: Find the pattern that holds across the performers. Individual interviews contain noise; the pattern is the signal. Keep only behaviors and skills that appear in at least three of the performers studied.

outputs.name: validated-pattern
outputs.desc: The behaviors and skills present in at least three of the performers studied

outputs.name: pattern-confidence
outputs.desc: For each kept item, the count of performers who exhibited it out of the total studied

process: Build a matrix with performers as rows and behaviors and hidden skills as columns, marking who exhibits each.
Count the frequency of each behavior and skill across the performers.
Keep only items present in three or more performers; the rest is individual variation.
Record the confidence for each kept item as the count out of the total performers studied.

steps.description: Rewrite the role requirements around the validated pattern. Replace guessed credentials with the behaviors and skills the best people actually use, and delete the requirements that predict nothing.

inputs.name: validated-pattern
inputs.desc: The behaviors and skills confirmed across performers

inputs.name: pattern-confidence
inputs.desc: How strong the evidence is for each

outputs.name: evidence-based-requirements
outputs.desc: The rewritten requirements, each stated in observable terms drawn from the validated pattern

outputs.name: removed-requirements
outputs.desc: The credential-noise requirements removed, with the reason each was cut

process: For each item in the validated pattern, write a requirement in observable terms, naming the behavior rather than a personality label.
Remove the credential-noise items, and state that you removed them and why, so the change is defensible.
Keep the requirement list short: the validated pattern, not a wish list.
Note that the new requirements will attract different applicants than the old ones, which is the intended result.

steps.description: Turn each evidence-based requirement into a screening signal you can observe in an application or a short conversation, so the pattern actually filters candidates instead of sitting in a document.

outputs.name: screening-questions
outputs.desc: A question or application signal for each requirement that strong candidates answer differently from weak ones

outputs.name: signal-scoring-key
outputs.desc: What a strong, average, and weak answer looks like for each question

process: For each requirement, write a screening question or application signal that a strong candidate answers differently from a weak one.
Replace vague prompts such as whether someone is a self-starter with behavioral prompts asking for a specific time they did something unasked.
Build a scoring key describing a strong, average, and weak answer for each question.
Test the questions on your known top performers; if they do not score high, the question is measuring the wrong thing.

description: Find the real levers of retention. Exit interviews are unreliable because people leaving soften the real reason. Survey current employees anonymously, cross-reference with departure data, and separate the stated reason from the real driver. Compensation is the stated reason roughly 70 percent of the time but the real driver only about 30 percent of the time, so fix the real drivers.

steps.description: Assemble departures over a defined window into structured records and look for clusters. A cluster is three or more departures that share a manager, a tenure band, a team, or a stated reason.

inputs.name: departure-records
inputs.desc: Raw records or notes for departures in the analysis window

inputs.name: analysis-window
inputs.desc: The time window to examine, such as the past 24 months

outputs.name: coded-departure-data
outputs.desc: Structured records with anonymized identity, stated reason, tenure, team, manager, role, and last rating

outputs.name: departure-clusters
outputs.desc: Groups of three or more departures sharing a common attribute, with managers above 1.5 times the base rate flagged

process: For each departure in the window, record anonymized identity, stated reason, tenure in months, team, manager, role, and last performance rating.
Group departures by manager, tenure band, team, and stated reason, and count each group.
Flag any group of three or more, and any manager whose departure rate runs above 1.5 times the company rate.
Note the data quality: what share of departures have complete records? Below 70 percent, the data carries a selection bias.

steps.description: Design a short anonymous pulse survey of current employees aimed at the clusters found in the departure data. Current employees say things departing ones soften, but only if anonymity is real.

outputs.name: pulse-survey
outputs.desc: Six to ten questions probing the suspected drivers behind each cluster, mixing scales with one open field

outputs.name: anonymity-protocol
outputs.desc: The practical anonymity rules, including never reporting any group smaller than five

process: Write six to ten questions that probe the suspected drivers behind each cluster, mixing rating scales with one open field.
Guarantee anonymity in practice: aggregate results so no group smaller than five is ever reported, and collect no identifying fields.
Target the survey at the teams and tenure bands where clusters appeared, plus a control group elsewhere for comparison.
Pilot the wording with a few trusted employees to confirm the questions read as neutral rather than leading.

steps.description: Separate the stated reason from the real driver by cross-referencing survey results with departure patterns. When four people leave the same manager citing four different reasons, the real driver is usually the manager, not four separate things.

outputs.name: stated-vs-driver-table
outputs.desc: For each cluster, the scattered stated reasons lined up against the consistent survey driver

outputs.name: driver-hypotheses
outputs.desc: A hypothesis for each cluster naming the real driver and the evidence for it

process: For each cluster, line up the stated reasons against the pulse survey results for that same team or tenure band.
Where stated reasons scatter but one survey driver is consistently low, treat that driver as the real cause.
Check whether the departures coincide with a change: a new manager, a reorg, a lost project, a policy shift.
Write a hypothesis for each cluster: the real driver is X, because the stated reasons scatter while the survey points to X.

steps.description: Rank the real drivers by the cost of leaving them unaddressed. Cost is the likely departures times the replacement cost, which runs from roughly 50 percent of annual salary for junior roles to 200 percent for senior ones.

inputs.name: stated-vs-driver-table
inputs.desc: The stated reasons against the real drivers

outputs.name: ranked-drivers
outputs.desc: The real drivers ranked by annual cost of inaction

outputs.name: cost-of-inaction
outputs.desc: For each driver, the estimated annual cost, with high performers counted separately

process: For each driver, estimate the departures per year it is likely causing from the cluster sizes.
Multiply by the replacement cost for that role level to get an annual cost of inaction.
Rank the drivers by annual cost; the most expensive driver is the first lever to pull.
Count high performers separately from low performers, since losing high performers to a driver costs more than the headcount alone suggests.

steps.description: For each top driver, select the lever that addresses it and check feasibility. A manager driver is fixed by coaching or reassignment, a growth-ceiling driver needs a new career path, a compensation driver needs a budget decision.

inputs.name: cost-of-inaction
inputs.desc: The annual cost of each driver

outputs.name: selected-levers
outputs.desc: The top three levers chosen, each matched to the driver it moves

outputs.name: feasibility-notes
outputs.desc: For each lever, its cost, timeline, and probability of working

process: Match each top driver to a specific lever that would actually move it, not a generic morale initiative.
Estimate each lever's cost, timeline, and probability of working.
Rank levers by expected return: cost of inaction times probability of success, minus the lever's cost.
Keep the top three levers; trying to pull every lever at once dilutes all of them.

steps.description: Turn each selected lever into a concrete intervention with an owner, a timeline, and a metric. A lever without a measurable target becomes a vague initiative that no one can judge.

outputs.name: intervention-plan
outputs.desc: For each lever, the specific change, its owner, the deadline, and the dependencies it needs

outputs.name: success-metrics
outputs.desc: The departure rate from each targeted cluster at six and twelve months, against a baseline

process: For each lever, state exactly what will change, who owns the change, and by when.
Define the success metric as the departure rate from the targeted cluster at six and twelve months.
Set a baseline from the departure data so you can measure movement.
Identify dependencies: approvals, budget, or other teams whose cooperation the lever needs.

steps.description: Track whether each intervention actually reduced departures from its targeted cluster. A drop of 30 percent or more at twelve months means the lever worked; no change means the hypothesis was wrong or the intervention was too weak.

outputs.name: outcome-report
outputs.desc: For each intervention, the before and after departure rate with a pass or fail at the 30 percent threshold

outputs.name: revised-driver-hypotheses
outputs.desc: For interventions that failed, the revised driver hypothesis and the next lever to try

process: At six months, count departures from each targeted cluster against the baseline window.
At twelve months, repeat; the twelve-month number is the one that decides.
A drop of 30 percent or more means the lever worked, so document it for reuse.
No change means the real driver was something else, so revise the hypothesis and pick the next lever.

description: Hire for what the team is missing, not for who already fits. Culture fit produces teams that agree on everything and share the same blind spots. Culture add produces teams that challenge each other. Map the team's strengths and gaps, define the culture-add profile, and evaluate candidates on what they bring that the team is short on.

steps.description: Map the team across professional background, problem-solving style, communication style, and experience, then mark where it has depth and where it is uniform. The aim is to see the team as a whole, not to label individuals.

inputs.name: team-roster
inputs.desc: The current team members and their backgrounds

inputs.name: team-mission
inputs.desc: What the team exists to accomplish and who it serves

outputs.name: strength-gap-map
outputs.desc: Where the team is deep and where it is thin or empty across the mapped dimensions

outputs.name: uniformity-flags
outputs.desc: Attributes shared by most of the team, marking where it is too uniform

process: For each team member, note background, problem-solving style, communication style, and relevant experience.
Look for clustering: any attribute shared by most of the team is a uniformity flag.
Ask, given the team's mission and who it serves, which perspectives are absent.
Produce a map showing where the team is deep and where it is thin or empty.

steps.description: Define what is missing as a profile, framed as perspectives and thinking styles rather than technical gaps. A team that only sees upside misses risk; a team of all specialists misses the generalist view.

inputs.name: strength-gap-map
inputs.desc: Where the team is deep and thin

inputs.name: uniformity-flags
inputs.desc: Where the team is too uniform

outputs.name: culture-add-profile
outputs.desc: The specific perspectives and thinking styles the team lacks, each with why it matters

outputs.name: blind-spot-examples
outputs.desc: Concrete cases where the team's uniformity caused a miss or a missed opportunity

process: For each uniformity flag, ask what it has caused the team to miss, and gather concrete examples.
Write each missing perspective with a reason it matters for this team's mission.
Record blind-spot examples as short stories: we shipped X without considering Y because no one had experience Z.
Rank the missing perspectives by how much filling each would improve the team's decisions.

steps.description: Convert the missing perspectives into screening criteria. The question shifts from whether a person is like us to whether they bring what we lack, which makes the decision evidence-based rather than a gut call.

outputs.name: add-criteria
outputs.desc: An observable criterion for each missing perspective

outputs.name: add-screening-questions
outputs.desc: A question for each criterion that candidates with the perspective answer differently

process: For each missing perspective, write an observable criterion, such as direct experience with a customer type the team does not understand.
For each criterion, write an interview question that a candidate with that perspective answers differently from one without it.
Confirm each question discriminates: if every candidate answers it the same way, rewrite it.
Keep the criteria tied to the profile, not to general likability.

steps.description: Design the interview so interviewers assess the specific contribution a candidate brings, not a general impression. The guide directs each interviewer to one or two criteria so the panel covers the whole profile.

outputs.name: interview-guide
outputs.desc: An assignment of one or two criteria to each interviewer, with the question and the evidence to listen for

outputs.name: contribution-evidence-form
outputs.desc: A form where interviewers record specific examples rather than adjectives

process: Assign each interviewer one or two criteria so no criterion is left unassessed and none is assessed five times.
For each criterion, give the interviewer the question and the evidence to listen for.
Build an evidence form where interviewers record specific examples, not adjectives.
Instruct interviewers to treat an unfamiliar style as a possible sign of the missing perspective, not an automatic negative.

steps.description: Guard against the pull toward similarity. Liking a candidate is a fit signal, not an add signal. A short checklist after each interview forces interviewers to separate their reaction from the evidence.

outputs.name: bias-checklist
outputs.desc: A post-interview checklist that separates reaction to similarity from evidence against criteria

outputs.name: debrief-protocol
outputs.desc: An evidence-first debrief where criteria are presented before any overall verdict

process: Build a checklist each interviewer completes after an interview: did I decide in the first five minutes, is my reaction about similarity or difference, can I name the criterion met or missed?
Run the debrief on evidence first: each interviewer presents examples against their assigned criteria before anyone gives an overall verdict.
Flag any verdict that rests on fit or feel with no criterion behind it, and send it back for evidence.
Record the assessment per criterion, then form the overall decision from the criteria, not the reverse.

steps.description: After the hire, check whether the added perspective actually changed outcomes. The proof is in decisions: did the team decide differently, or catch a blind spot it would have missed? Track this for the first twelve months.

outputs.name: add-impact-log
outputs.desc: Specific instances where the added perspective changed a decision or caught a blind spot in the first twelve months

outputs.name: profile-adjustments
outputs.desc: Changes to the culture-add profile for the next hire based on the log

process: At monthly retrospectives, ask whether anyone's different perspective changed a decision this month.
Log each instance: the decision, what the team would have done without the input, and what the perspective added.
At twelve months, review the log; several logged instances mean the criteria were good.
If the log is empty, either the criteria missed or the team did not make room for the perspective, so adjust the profile for the next hire.

description: Decide what to delegate, to whom, and when. Score each task on two axes: does it require your specific expertise, and is it among the highest-value uses of your time? Tasks low on both are the first to delegate. Define the outcome rather than the process, give real authority, and set a check-in cadence that matches the person's experience.

steps.description: Score every recurring task on two axes: does it require your specific expertise, and is it among the highest-value uses of your time? Tasks low on both axes are delegation candidates.

inputs.name: task-inventory
inputs.desc: Every recurring task you personally perform

inputs.name: time-log
inputs.desc: How much time each task takes per week

outputs.name: scored-task-grid
outputs.desc: Each task placed on a two-by-two of expertise required against value of your time spent

outputs.name: delegation-candidates
outputs.desc: The low-expertise, low-value tasks that form the delegation pool

process: List every recurring task you personally do, with the hours each takes per week.
Score each task on expertise required, meaning only you can do it versus many could, and on the value of your time spent on it.
Place each task on a two-by-two grid.
The low-expertise, low-value quadrant is the delegation candidate pool; the high-expertise, high-value quadrant is what you keep.

steps.description: Narrow the candidate pool to the tasks worth delegating first. Not every low-value task is ready to hand off; some need documentation, and some are too tangled with judgment to transfer cleanly yet.

outputs.name: delegation-shortlist
outputs.desc: The tasks to delegate now, ranked by the time each frees

outputs.name: retained-tasks
outputs.desc: The tasks kept, confirmed as genuinely high-expertise or high-value

process: From the candidate pool, flag tasks that recur often enough that delegating them frees real time.
Set aside tasks that cannot be delegated until they are documented, and note what each needs.
Confirm the retained tasks are genuinely high-expertise or high-value, not just tasks you enjoy.
Produce a shortlist of tasks to delegate now, ranked by the time each frees.

steps.description: Match each shortlisted task to a person and assess that person's readiness for it. Readiness sets the check-in cadence later: a person new to a task needs more contact, a proven one needs less.

outputs.name: task-person-matches
outputs.desc: Each task matched to a person who could take it

outputs.name: readiness-levels
outputs.desc: Each person's readiness for the matched task: new, has done parts, or has done it before

process: For each task, identify who could take it, favoring people with adjacent skills and room to grow.
Rate each person's readiness for the task: new to it, has done parts of it, or has done it before.
Avoid overloading one person with several single-point tasks at once.
Record each task-person match with its readiness level.

steps.description: For each delegated task, define the outcome rather than the process. Specifying the result and the boundaries, then leaving the method to the person, is what makes delegation develop people instead of creating remote-controlled hands.

outputs.name: outcome-statements
outputs.desc: Each delegation written as an observable outcome rather than a list of steps

outputs.name: boundary-conditions
outputs.desc: The budget, deadlines, and decision limits for each delegated task

process: Write each delegation as an outcome: what good looks like when done, in observable terms, not a list of steps.
State the boundaries: budget, deadlines, decisions they can make alone, and decisions that need you.
Name the resources available to them, including who they can ask when stuck.
Confirm the outcome is specific enough that both of you would agree whether it was met.

steps.description: Give real authority with each task. Delegating responsibility without authority sets the person up to fail and pulls the work back to you. State what they can decide, spend, and commit to on their own.

outputs.name: authority-grants
outputs.desc: The decisions, spending, and commitments each person now owns outright

outputs.name: escalation-rules
outputs.desc: The specific situations where the person must come to you before acting

process: For each task, state the decisions the person now owns outright.
State the spending and commitments they can make without checking first.
Define the escalation rule: the specific situations where they must come to you before acting.
Communicate the authority to anyone else who needs to honor it, so the person is not second-guessed by peers.

steps.description: Set the check-in cadence by the person's readiness, not by your anxiety. A person new to a task checks in often at first, then less as they prove reliable; a proven person checks in on results only.

outputs.name: checkin-schedule
outputs.desc: The check-in frequency and focus for each task, matched to readiness

outputs.name: cadence-rationale
outputs.desc: The plan to loosen the cadence as the person proves reliable, so they can see the path to full ownership

process: For a person new to a task, schedule frequent short check-ins early, focused on approach, then widen the interval as they show competence.
For a proven person, check in on outcomes at natural milestones, not on method.
Make check-ins about removing obstacles and confirming direction, not inspecting every step.
Record the cadence and the plan to loosen it, so the person can see the path to full ownership.

steps.description: Review how the delegation went and feed the result into the next round. Delegation set once and never reviewed either drifts or snaps back to you, and the review also tells you what to delegate next.

outputs.name: delegation-review
outputs.desc: For each delegated task, whether the outcome was met and whether the authority and cadence fit

outputs.name: next-delegation-set
outputs.desc: The freed time and the next tasks to delegate, starting again from the task grid

process: At the first natural endpoint, review each delegated task: was the outcome met, and did the authority and cadence fit?
Where a task snapped back to you, find why: an unclear outcome, missing authority, or a readiness mismatch.
Loosen the cadence on tasks the person now owns reliably, and move them toward the next task.
Add newly freed time to the next delegation round, starting again from the task grid.

description: Deliver feedback with the Situation-Behavior-Impact method. Name the specific situation, describe the observable behavior, and state its impact, within about 48 hours while the memory is fresh. Ask for the other person's view, agree on one specific change, and follow up in a week.

steps.description: Decide whether an event is worth feedback and how fast it must be delivered. Not every observation needs feedback, but anything that should repeat or should stop does, and it should land within about 48 hours.

inputs.name: observed-event
inputs.desc: The event you are considering giving feedback on

inputs.name: feedback-goal
inputs.desc: The outcome you care about that the behavior helps or hurts

outputs.name: feedback-worthiness
outputs.desc: Whether the event warrants feedback, and whether the intent is to reinforce or to redirect

outputs.name: timing-window
outputs.desc: The delivery window, within about 48 hours and in private

process: Check the event against the goal: does this behavior help or hurt the result you care about?
Decide the intent: reinforce a behavior you want repeated, or redirect one you want changed. Both use the same method.
If the event is trivial or a one-off with no pattern, let it go rather than diluting your feedback.
Set the delivery window within about 48 hours, in private, while both of you remember the specifics.

steps.description: Build the feedback as a Situation-Behavior-Impact statement. Name the specific situation, describe the observable behavior without interpretation, and state the concrete impact, which keeps the feedback factual rather than a character judgment.

outputs.name: sbi-statement
outputs.desc: The feedback written as situation, then observable behavior, then concrete impact

outputs.name: evidence-notes
outputs.desc: The specific observations behind the statement, stripped of motive-reading

process: Write the situation: the specific time and place, so the person can picture the moment.
Write the behavior as what you observed, not what you assume they intended, such as that they interrupted twice rather than that they were dismissive.
Write the impact: what resulted, for the work, the team, or you.
Strip out labels and motive-reading; the statement should be something the person could have seen on a recording.

steps.description: Plan when and where to deliver the feedback. Reinforcing feedback can be fairly public; redirecting feedback is always private. The setting and timing shape whether the message lands or triggers defense.

outputs.name: delivery-plan
outputs.desc: The chosen time, medium, and opening line that leads with the situation

outputs.name: setting-choice
outputs.desc: The setting: private for redirecting feedback, either for reinforcing

process: Choose the setting: private for redirecting feedback, and either private or public for reinforcing feedback depending on the person.
Pick a time inside the window when the person can absorb it, not right before a high-pressure moment.
Plan your opening line so it leads with the situation, not with a verdict.
Decide the medium: in person or a live call for anything sensitive, never a one-way written message for redirecting feedback.

steps.description: After delivering the statement, ask for the person's perspective before moving to solutions. They may have context you lack, and asking turns the feedback into a conversation rather than a verdict.

outputs.name: elicitation-questions
outputs.desc: An open question to hand the conversation over and surface the person's view

outputs.name: listening-plan
outputs.desc: The plan to listen fully and to adjust if their context changes the picture

process: Prepare an open question to hand the conversation over, such as how they saw the situation.
Plan to listen fully before responding, and to take their context seriously if it changes the picture.
Prepare for common reactions such as surprise, disagreement, or over-apology, and how you will keep the conversation on the behavior.
Decide what you will do if their perspective shows your read was wrong: adjust, rather than defend the original statement.

steps.description: Agree on one specific change, not a vague promise to do better. The change should be observable, so that in a week both of you can tell whether it happened.

inputs.name: elicitation-questions
inputs.desc: The questions used to surface their view

outputs.name: agreed-change
outputs.desc: A single observable change the person will make, stated in terms of what they will do differently

outputs.name: change-owner
outputs.desc: Who owns the change and what support they need from you to make it

process: Narrow to a single specific change rather than a list, so it is achievable.
State the change in observable terms: what the person will do differently next time, in what situation.
Confirm the person agrees it is reasonable and owns it, rather than accepting it only to end the conversation.
Name any support they need from you to make the change, and commit to providing it.

steps.description: Schedule the follow-up for about a week out and hold it. Feedback without follow-up signals that the change did not really matter, and the follow-up is where reinforcement and accountability happen.

inputs.name: change-owner
inputs.desc: Who owns it and the support promised

outputs.name: followup-schedule
outputs.desc: The follow-up set about a week out, checking the observable change

outputs.name: outcome-note
outputs.desc: What happened at the follow-up and the next step if the change did not stick

process: Set the follow-up about a week out, while the agreed change is still fresh and testable.
At the follow-up, check against the observable change: did it happen in the situations where it should have?
If it happened, reinforce it specifically so the person knows it was noticed.
If it did not, revisit whether the change was clear, achievable, and supported, and adjust rather than simply repeating the feedback.

description: Run one-on-ones as the direct report's meeting, not the manager's status update. The report sets the agenda; the manager removes obstacles and develops the person. A simple structure of roughly ten minutes on priorities, ten on blockers, and ten on growth keeps it balanced, and each side ends with one commitment that is tracked across meetings.

steps.description: Set the charter for the one-on-one so both sides understand its purpose. The meeting belongs to the report, is not a status update, and exists to remove obstacles and develop the person.

inputs.name: manager-report-pair
inputs.desc: The manager and direct report who hold the meeting

inputs.name: current-practice
inputs.desc: How their one-on-ones run today, if at all

outputs.name: meeting-charter
outputs.desc: The written purpose: the report's meeting, for obstacles and growth, not a status review

outputs.name: cadence-decision
outputs.desc: The agreed frequency and the commitment to protect the slot from casual cancellation

process: State the purpose in writing: the report's meeting, for obstacles and growth, not a project status review.
Agree the cadence, weekly for most and biweekly for very experienced reports, and protect the slot from casual cancellation.
Agree that status reporting happens in another channel so this time is not consumed by updates.
Set the expectation that the report brings the agenda.

steps.description: Give the report a simple way to build the agenda before each meeting. When the report prepares, the meeting is about what they need; when they do not, it drifts back to a manager monologue.

outputs.name: agenda-template
outputs.desc: A short shared agenda the report fills in before each meeting

outputs.name: prep-prompts
outputs.desc: Prompts that cue the report toward priorities, blockers, and growth

process: Provide a short shared agenda the report fills in before each meeting.
Include prompts: what do you want to prioritize, what is blocking you, where do you want to grow.
Ask the report to add items as they come up during the week, so nothing waits for memory.
Let the manager add at most one or two items, clearly marked, so the meeting stays the report's.

steps.description: Structure the meeting into three rough blocks: priorities, blockers, and growth. The blocks keep the conversation from being consumed entirely by this week's fires and never reaching development.

outputs.name: time-block-structure
outputs.desc: The division of the meeting into priorities, blockers, and growth blocks

outputs.name: block-guidance
outputs.desc: What belongs in each block and the rule to protect the growth block

process: Allocate roughly a third of the time to priorities: what matters most for the report now and whether it is on track.
Allocate roughly a third to blockers: what is in the way and what the manager can remove.
Allocate roughly a third to growth: skills, career, and development, which is the block fires usually crowd out.
Keep the blocks flexible but protect the growth block, since it is the one with no deadline forcing it.

steps.description: Capture the obstacles the report raises and track the manager's actions to remove them. The manager's main job in the meeting is to clear the path, and an untracked obstacle signals that raising them is pointless.

outputs.name: obstacle-list
outputs.desc: Each obstacle the report raises, carried forward until removed

outputs.name: manager-action-items
outputs.desc: The actions only the manager can take to clear each obstacle, with owners and dates

process: During the blockers block, write down each obstacle the report raises.
For each, decide who can remove it and by when, with the manager taking the items only the manager can act on.
Carry open obstacles forward to the next meeting rather than letting them disappear.
Close the loop visibly: when an obstacle is removed, note it so the report sees that raising it worked.

steps.description: End each meeting with one commitment from each side. A single concrete commitment each turns the conversation into action and makes the next meeting's follow-up obvious.

outputs.name: commitment-pair
outputs.desc: One concrete commitment from the report and one from the manager before the next meeting

outputs.name: commitment-log
outputs.desc: Both commitments recorded where both sides can see them

process: Before closing, agree one commitment the report will make and one the manager will make before the next meeting.
Keep each to a single concrete action, not a list, so it actually gets done.
Record both commitments where both sides can see them.
Make the commitments specific enough that at the next meeting it is clear whether each happened.

steps.description: Keep a running log across meetings so one-on-ones build on each other instead of restarting weekly. The log is also where patterns show up: a blocker that never clears, a growth goal that never advances.

outputs.name: continuity-record
outputs.desc: One running document per report holding agendas, obstacles, and commitments, newest on top

outputs.name: pattern-signals
outputs.desc: Recurring blockers and stalled growth goals surfaced by reading across meetings

process: Maintain one running document per report, newest entry on top, holding agendas, obstacles, and commitments.
Start each meeting by checking the previous commitments and open obstacles.
Watch for patterns across weeks: a recurring blocker points to a system problem, a stalled growth goal points to crowding-out.
Review the log before development and career conversations, since it is the record of what actually happened week to week.

description: Map the skills the work requires against who actually has them. Any skill held by only one person at a competent level is a single point of failure; any skill held by no one is a gap. Cross-train the single points of failure, and hire, train, or contract for the gaps.

steps.description: List the skills the work actually requires by deriving them from recent tasks, not from job descriptions. Include technical, process, and relationship skills, since the person who alone knows how to handle a key vendor is also a single point of failure.

inputs.name: recent-work-log
inputs.desc: The tasks the team performed over the last quarter

outputs.name: required-skill-list
outputs.desc: The skills the work requires, derived from actual tasks at a specific level

outputs.name: skill-categories
outputs.desc: The skills grouped into technical, process, relationship, and domain-knowledge categories

process: List every distinct task the team performed over the last quarter, grouping similar tasks.
For each task group, name the skills required to do it, at a specific level rather than a broad category.
Include relationship and knowledge skills, such as who the key vendor trusts or who understands a legacy system.
Group the skills into technical, process, relationship, and domain-knowledge categories.

steps.description: Build a matrix of who can do each skill and at what level: learning, competent, or expert. Use self-assessment checked against peer assessment, since self-assessment alone is unreliable.

outputs.name: coverage-matrix
outputs.desc: A matrix of team members by skill, each cell holding learning, competent, or expert

outputs.name: confidence-notes
outputs.desc: Cells flagged low-confidence where self and peer assessments diverge

process: Ask each team member to rate themselves on each skill: learning, competent, or expert.
For each skill, ask one or two peers to confirm whether they would trust this person to handle a task needing it alone.
Where self and peer ratings diverge, default to the peer rating and flag the cell as low-confidence.
Record the matrix with team members as rows, skills as columns, and the level in each cell.

steps.description: Scan the matrix for single points of failure: skills where only one person is competent or above. If that person is out, the team cannot perform that function. Rank the single points by how often the skill is needed and what happens when it is unavailable.

outputs.name: single-point-list
outputs.desc: Every skill with exactly one person at competent or above

outputs.name: spof-impact-ranking
outputs.desc: The single points ranked by frequency of need times consequence of unavailability

process: For each skill, count the people at competent or above.
A count of one is a single point of failure, so record each one.
For each single point, estimate how often the skill is needed and what happens when the person is unavailable: work stops, quality drops, or a workaround exists.
Rank the single points by frequency times consequence; daily need and work stopping is the highest priority.

steps.description: Find the skills with zero people at competent or above. These are gaps the team is either not doing or doing badly, often hidden behind workarounds. Rank them by the cost of the function going uncovered.

outputs.name: gap-list
outputs.desc: Every skill with no one at competent or above, with how the function is handled now

outputs.name: gap-impact-ranking
outputs.desc: The gaps ranked by the cost of the function going uncovered

process: Scan the matrix for skills with a count of zero at competent or above.
For each, determine how the function is handled now: a workaround, an external contractor, or not at all.
Estimate the cost of the gap: what breaks or is left undone because no one owns the skill.
Rank the gaps by that cost, so the most damaging uncovered function comes first.

steps.description: Decide, for each single point and gap, whether to cross-train, hire, or contract. Single points are usually solved by cross-training; gaps need a hire, a trained-up person, or a contractor, depending on how specialized the skill is.

outputs.name: remediation-decisions
outputs.desc: For each single point and gap, the chosen path: cross-train, hire, train, or contract

outputs.name: decision-rationale
outputs.desc: The reason behind each decision

process: For each single point of failure, check whether someone with adjacent skills can be cross-trained; if so, cross-train is the default.
For each gap, decide: train an existing person if the skill is learnable in reasonable time, hire if it is core and ongoing, contract if it is specialized and intermittent.
Avoid cross-training a person who is already a single point on another skill, since that just moves the risk.
Record the decision and the reason for each single point and gap.

steps.description: Turn the decisions into a plan with owners, timelines, and a review cadence. Skills change as the work changes, so a matrix left to age becomes unreliable within a couple of quarters.

outputs.name: remediation-plan
outputs.desc: For each decision, the owner, the target, and what competent looks like, sequenced by impact

outputs.name: review-cadence
outputs.desc: A quarterly review to reassess levels, add new skills, and re-scan for single points and gaps

process: For each cross-training decision, name who learns, who teaches, what competent looks like, and a realistic target date.
For each hire or contract decision, name the owner and the trigger to start.
Sequence the plan by the impact rankings, addressing the highest-impact single points and gaps first.
Set a quarterly review to reassess levels, add new skills from recent work, and re-scan for new single points and gaps.

description: Calibrate performance ratings across managers so the rating reflects the employee, not the rater. Bring managers together with anonymized rated examples, have them rate independently, and compare. Where they diverge, discuss the criteria until they agree, and document the calibrated criteria with concrete examples for next time.

steps.description: Assemble a set of anonymized work examples that span the rating scale. These shared examples are what managers will rate independently, so they must be stripped of identity and cover the range from weak to exceptional.

inputs.name: rating-cycle-scope
inputs.desc: The team and cycle being calibrated

inputs.name: work-samples
inputs.desc: Real work examples available from across the team

outputs.name: example-set
outputs.desc: Anonymized examples spanning the full scale, including borderline cases between levels

outputs.name: example-answer-key
outputs.desc: A private record of how each example was originally rated, held back from the managers for now

process: Collect real work examples from across the team that represent different performance levels.
Strip every example of names, teams, and identifying detail so no manager recognizes the author.
Choose a set that spans the full scale, including borderline cases between levels, since those are where calibration matters most.
Record a private key of how each example was originally rated, to compare against later, without showing it to the managers yet.

steps.description: Have each manager rate the same examples alone, before any discussion. Independent rating first exposes real disagreement; discussing before rating lets the loudest voice set the anchor.

outputs.name: independent-ratings
outputs.desc: Each manager's rating of every example, submitted before any discussion

outputs.name: rating-spread
outputs.desc: The spread per example, showing where managers agree and where they scatter

process: Give every manager the same anonymized example set and the rating scale.
Have each manager rate every example alone, with no discussion, and submit before the session.
Collect all ratings and compute the spread per example: where managers agree and where they scatter.
Keep the ratings attributed privately so you can see which managers run high or low, without exposing it in the room.

steps.description: Find where the managers diverge and whether any manager leans systematically high or low. A single example rated across three levels is a criteria problem; a manager who rates everything high is a leniency problem.

outputs.name: divergence-cases
outputs.desc: The widest-scatter examples, set as the agenda for discussion

outputs.name: systematic-lean-flags
outputs.desc: Managers whose average runs systematically above or below the group

process: Sort the examples by how widely the ratings scatter; the widest-scatter examples are the first to discuss.
For each manager, compare their average rating against the group average to flag systematic leniency or severity.
Separate the two problems: examples that scatter point to unclear criteria, managers who lean point to individual bias.
Prepare the divergence cases and lean flags as the agenda for the calibration discussion.

steps.description: Facilitate the discussion of the divergent cases. The facilitator does not overrule managers; they ask managers to justify ratings with evidence from the example until the group converges on what each level means.

inputs.name: systematic-lean-flags
inputs.desc: The managers who lean high or low

outputs.name: discussion-record
outputs.desc: The reasoning that settled each divergent case

outputs.name: resolved-ratings
outputs.desc: The agreed rating for each divergent case after discussion

process: Start with the widest-scatter example, asking managers at the high and low ends to point to the specific evidence behind their rating.
Compare examples across levels: if a high example has weaker evidence than a meets example, the ratings are inconsistent and the group adjusts.
Keep the discussion on the criteria, not on defending a number, asking what specifically separates one level from the next.
Record the resolved rating for each divergent case and the reasoning that settled it.

steps.description: Document the calibrated criteria with the anchor examples the group agreed on. Written criteria with concrete examples let the next cycle start calibrated instead of relitigating every level.

outputs.name: calibrated-criteria
outputs.desc: What each rating level means in observable terms, drawn from the discussion

outputs.name: anchor-examples
outputs.desc: A concrete anonymized example attached to each level

process: For each rating level, write what it means in observable terms, drawn from the discussion.
Attach an anchor example to each level: a concrete anonymized case the group agreed represents it.
Capture the distinctions that caused the most disagreement, since those are where raters drift.
Distribute the calibrated criteria and anchors to all managers before the next rating cycle.

steps.description: Monitor whether ratings stay calibrated over cycles. If the independent ratings scatter less each cycle, calibration is working; if they scatter the same or more, the criteria are not being used or the examples have gone stale.

outputs.name: drift-report
outputs.desc: The rating spread each cycle compared against prior cycles

outputs.name: criteria-updates
outputs.desc: Revisions to the criteria and anchors where the same distinctions keep causing scatter

process: Each cycle, repeat the independent rating on a fresh example set and measure the spread.
Compare the spread against prior cycles; a narrowing spread means calibration is holding.
Where the same distinctions keep causing scatter, revise the criteria and anchor examples to address them.
Refresh the example set periodically so managers calibrate against current work, not old cases.

description: Make the firing decision by separating a skill problem, where the person cannot do the work, from a will problem, where the person will not. For a skill problem, confirm you gave clear expectations, training, and time. For a will problem, confirm you gave clear expectations, feedback, and consequences. If you have done both and the gap persists, the decision is made for you, and you execute it directly, specifically, immediately, and humanely.

steps.description: Diagnose whether the problem is skill, meaning the person cannot do the work, or will, meaning they choose not to. The two look similar from the outside but need opposite responses, and mistaking one for the other wastes months.

inputs.name: performance-concern
inputs.desc: The specific performance concern prompting the review

inputs.name: performance-record
inputs.desc: The history of expectations, feedback, and results for this person

outputs.name: problem-diagnosis
outputs.desc: Whether the gap is skill, will, or a mix

outputs.name: supporting-evidence
outputs.desc: The cases of trying and falling short, or being able and not doing, behind the diagnosis

process: State the specific performance gap in observable terms, not as a judgment of the person.
Ask the skill question: when the person genuinely tries, can they produce the result? Look for cases where they tried and still fell short.
Ask the will question: when the person is capable, do they consistently choose to do it? Look for cases where they could and did not.
Diagnose skill, will, or a mix, and record the evidence behind the call.

steps.description: For a skill problem, check whether the person was actually given a fair path: clear expectations, real training, and enough time to reach competence. If any of these was missing, the problem may be yours to fix before it is theirs to answer for.

inputs.name: problem-diagnosis
inputs.desc: The skill, will, or mixed diagnosis

outputs.name: skill-path-finding
outputs.desc: Whether clear expectations, real training, and enough time were provided

outputs.name: skill-remedy-gaps
outputs.desc: Any missing element of the skill path that must be provided before the gap is treated as unfixable

process: Confirm expectations were stated clearly and specifically, not assumed.
Confirm real training or support was provided, not just a one-time explanation.
Confirm enough time was given to reach competence at this skill, by a realistic standard for its difficulty.
Where any element was missing, provide it and reset the clock before treating the gap as unfixable.

steps.description: For a will problem, check whether the person was given clear expectations, direct feedback on the gap, and real consequences for not closing it. A will problem that never met a consequence has not actually been tested.

inputs.name: skill-path-finding
inputs.desc: Whether the skill path was adequate

outputs.name: will-path-finding
outputs.desc: Whether clear expectations, direct feedback, and real consequences were provided

outputs.name: will-remedy-gaps
outputs.desc: Any missing element of the will path that must be delivered before deciding

process: Confirm expectations were clear, so the person knew exactly what was required.
Confirm the gap was named directly in feedback, not hinted at or softened into invisibility.
Confirm a real consequence followed the continued gap, so the person understood it mattered.
Where feedback or consequence was missing, deliver it clearly and give a defined window to respond before deciding.

steps.description: Pass the case through the decision gate. If the person was given the full path for their problem type and the gap still persists, the decision is made for you. If the path had holes, the gate sends you back to fill them first.

inputs.name: will-path-finding
inputs.desc: Whether the will path was adequate

outputs.name: decision-determination
outputs.desc: Whether to separate now or to close a path gap and reassess

outputs.name: decision-record
outputs.desc: The path provided and the evidence of the persistent gap, recorded for fairness and defensibility

process: Check that the adequate path for the diagnosed problem type was fully provided: training and time for skill, feedback and consequence for will.
If any element was missing, do not decide to separate yet; close the gap and reassess after a defined period.
If the full path was provided and the gap persists at the agreed standard, the determination is to separate.
Record the determination with the path provided and the evidence of the persistent gap, which is fair to the person and sound if later questioned.

steps.description: Plan the separation to be direct, specific, immediate, and humane. Dragging it out, softening it into ambiguity, or ambushing the person all make it worse, and the person should already know the gap and the consequences from prior feedback.

outputs.name: separation-plan
outputs.desc: The timing, privacy, support offered, and who is present, planned with dignity

outputs.name: communication-script
outputs.desc: A short script that states the decision first and does not relitigate the whole history

process: Confirm the person has already heard the gap and the consequences in prior feedback, so the decision is not a surprise.
Plan to deliver it directly and specifically: the decision, the reason in one or two clear sentences, and that it is final.
Plan the logistics with dignity: timing, privacy, what support such as notice, references, or transition help is offered, and who is present.
Write a short script that states the decision first and does not relitigate the whole history.

steps.description: Repair the team after a separation. A departure the team saw coming can restore trust if handled openly within privacy limits; one handled clumsily makes everyone wonder if they are next. Cover the work and address the team without disparaging the person.

outputs.name: team-communication
outputs.desc: What the team is told, promptly and plainly, without private details or disparagement

outputs.name: workload-plan
outputs.desc: Who absorbs the departed person's work temporarily and the timeline to backfill or redistribute

process: Tell the team promptly and plainly that the person has left, without sharing private details or disparaging them.
Reassure the team about what happens to the departed person's work and that the process was fair.
Plan the coverage: who absorbs what temporarily, and the timeline to backfill or redistribute.
Watch for the team's response: strong performers who were carrying the gap should feel relief, not new fear.
